He dismisses the optimistic scenario of rates being cut soon and growth rebounding as not being on the cards. He argues policymakers have focused too much on redistribution rather than policies that lift productivity, and this structural weakness is now hitting hard.
quote: a tricky spot to be in that, you know, if my story is the right take and growth is actually quite sluggish and tomorrow's print is on the weak side, then really you've got this combination where inflation is too high and growth is already very weak. And you might as go as far as saying it's sort of stagflation. You know, the economy's not growing, but actually inflation is proving to be stubbornly, stubbornly, stubbornly elevated. And the alternative story which others might run is that, oh, well, the print is going to be okay, but it's actually holding up okay. In which case the answer is, well then the RBA probably actually given it's got high inflation and growth, it's got momentum, has to push the economy into a bigger downturn to get inflation down. And so threatens or risks driving the economy into a recession. You know, I think in if you're thinking about the pace at which house prices are declining at the moment and the fact that the RBA, if they do lift rates further, there's a reasonable chance is growing that actually they have to push the economy into a recession to get inflation down. And if you think about those two combinations, either we're in a state inflationary and either we're sort of in a stagflation free space or the economy is typically, you know, got some risk of tipping into a recession.
